home.name: Home
home.change: The hero headline is now the client's slogan, Engineering Precision. Delivering Excellence., with More about us as the button (14 Oct, IAQ). The seven-market rail under the hero is gone. The numbers band carries IAQ's new figures (530+ employees, 85% engineering workforce, 20 tons of carbon, 235+ projects). Tool Installation is stage 5 and Maintenance stage 6 (Sunny, 13 Oct). The Scroll to build 3D is the client's requested home 3D, on a 16,000 px scroll runway with a skip button. The markets band says Seven markets, one integrated team.

design.why: The hero reads well on its own: the two-line headline sits low over the lift photograph and the red word lands. But the seven-market rail that tied the hero to the markets is gone, so the first screen no longer says who IAQ builds for. The 3D section runs 16,000 px of scroll for one stage, which is 60 percent of the page; a visitor who does not want it scrolls through four blank screens before reaching the markets. The numbers band and the cycle ring are the 9 Oct design unchanged.

copy.why: Engineering Precision. Delivering Excellence. is a claim any contractor can make; the 9 Oct line said what IAQ builds (the environments where the future is made) and the lede said what it is (cleanrooms, dry rooms and the systems that hold them in spec). The new lede is one 20-word sentence of category words: integrated engineering, total facility solutions, complex industrial, mission-critical. Title case on a slogan is against the house. If the slogan is the client's, keep it and give it a lede that names the product and the figure (31 years, one team).

home.fix: Put the seven-market rail back under the hero. Cap the 3D runway at six screens or make the stage advance on its own with the scroll as a scrub. Rewrite the lede figure first; keep the slogan only if IAQ insists.

fixed.what: The Scroll to build runway is capped at eight screens, from twenty-one. The build still runs every step, the scrub is faster, the skip button stays.
fixed.why: Sixty percent of the page was blank scroll under one stage. The client asked for a skip button on 12 Oct, a sign the length cost them; the cap keeps the 3D and every step and shortens the wait.
fixed.held: The headline and the statement are IAQ's 19 Oct text and the seven-market rail left on IAQ's 9 Oct word ("remove that", "keep the position but remove the service"); both stay. The statement rewrite is proposed below.

proposals.why: Names the product and the figure; no category words. The headline above it stays IAQ's.

proposals.now: Complex facilities require more than technical expertise. They demand seamless coordination across engineering, procurement and construction to ensure every element is aligned from concept to commissioning. Through an integrated project delivery approach, IAQ combines multidisciplinary expertise, meticulous planning and disciplined execution to deliver facilities that meet the highest standards of quality.
proposals.proposed: One contract covers engineering, procurement and construction, so one team answers for the facility from concept to commissioning. IAQ's engineers, project managers and construction staff plan and run the work together, and the facility is handed over proven, not promised.
proposals.why: The same claim in half the words, a verb in every sentence, no seamless or meticulous.

proposals.now: IAQ delivers EPC solutions through a multidisciplinary team of engineers, project managers and construction professionals. Our capabilities span the full project lifecycle, enabling efficient coordination and successful project delivery across complex industrial environments.
proposals.proposed: Six capabilities, one team: engineering and design, procurement, construction, process utilities, tool installation, testing and commissioning. Every one is carried in house.
proposals.why: Lists what the six are, so the sentence can be checked against the grid under it.

proposals.now: Enhanced Coordination. Reduced Project Complexity. Improved Schedule Certainty. Quality & Safety Focus. Operational Readiness. Each with a line of the same shape (improved collaboration..., a structured delivery framework..., early planning..., consistent management..., a lifecycle approach...).
proposals.proposed: Coordination: design, procurement and construction sit with one team, so a change in one is known to the others the same day. Less complexity: one framework for decisions, one programme, one point of contact. Schedule certainty: long-lead items are ordered from design sign-off, so the programme is set before site starts. Quality and safety: one management system, ISO 9001, 14001 and 45001, across every phase. Operational readiness: commissioning is in the contract, so the facility is handed over running.
proposals.why: IAQ's five reasons in IAQ's order; each now carries the mechanism or the standard behind it. Sentence case.

proposals.now: Whether planning a new facility, expanding existing operations or upgrading critical infrastructure, IAQ delivers integrated EPC solutions that transform complex requirements into operationally ready facilities.
proposals.proposed: A new facility, an extension or an upgrade: send the brief and the programme, and one team takes it from design to handover.
proposals.why: The ask is in the sentence. 29 words to 23.

IAQ delivers integrated PCU and TTI solutions that connect critical utility infrastructure with manufacturing tools, enabling a seamless transition from facility completion to operational readiness.
proposals.proposed: A fab is ready when every tool is connected to its gases, chemicals, water, power and exhaust, and proven. IAQ builds those utilities and brings each one to the tool, so the gap between a finished building and a producing line is closed by one team.
proposals.why: Says what the utilities are; keeps IAQ's readiness idea; 42 words to 46 but every one a noun or a verb.

rules.rule: A description that runs to two lines is balanced: two lines of near-equal length, never one long and one short.
Air between a description and its button: the button sits a clear step below the text.
A title must mean something a reader can take away. Not a label of what the block is (in numbers) but a statement the block proves.
Figures and their icons are not a list: display-size numbers, a mark beside each, a label under, so the record reads as proof.
A stage readout shows the stage number only, never 3 / 6.
Every panel is part of the page: a card with the page's own button and a way to continue (next, previous), never a floating node with a text link.
Icons are the isometric set. The older photoreal and line marks are replaced wherever they still stand.
No full stop at the end of a title. Commas are fine, they carry meaning.
rules.from: Home markets band, 22 Oct; applied to every title on the site

rules.rule: A line break falls where a thought ends. A description that is split in two tones breaks before the second thought, never with its first word dangling.
No repeated information in one view. Repeated design is fine, it is consistency; repeated content is not.
Menu hover: the word goes a touch heavier and red. No dot, no marker.
A dropdown has no coloured outline; a neutral hairline and a shadow.
Every button and icon answers the pointer: colour, a one-pixel lift, a darker button.

Type sizes: body text on Tony Robbins' site measures 20 px, nav 16 px. IAQ runs 15 px body and 18.5 px ledes at a 1.12 zoom (about 17 and 21 px on screen). Decision pending: a body step up to 16 or 17 px.
An inner page banner is not the home banner: about half the window, never the full height.
No white fade or blur on a banner. The picture ends where the section ends.
On every page that opens on a dark banner the bar runs clear at the top and goes solid on scroll, as on the home page.
A proof block (certificates, awards) is centred: title, the marks, the line and the link in the middle, with room above and below.
The member area is designed in every state: signed out, wrong passcode, signed in, the portal, the gate, signed out again. Actions in sentence case.
A small-caps label keeps its style but not its tracking: letter-spacing.04em at most, site wide. Wide tracking reads as scattered.
The orphan wrap: a caption, a label or a one-sentence line never breaks into a second line of one or two words. It runs the full width of what it sits under, or it is one line.

A timeline shows the flow of time: an axis that draws as it is read, the passed marks filled, the live one lit, the year at reading size. Unless the layout is responsive and there really is no room (a phone), where a short last line is allowed.
No standalone illustration where a photograph of IAQ's own work exists.
A breadcrumb sits at the top of the banner, under the bar, never at its foot above the title.
A figure that is the point of the page (the years) is set at display size, not as a small label.
Say a thing once per page: a hero line is not repeated as a foot heading. Where the foot needs a heading, give it the figure.
& in a title only where it joins two names (Engineering, Procurement & Construction; Food & Beverage); "and" inside a sentence title.
A two-part title breaks before its red phrase: the statement on one line, the phrase on the next, never mid-phrase. The same for the description under it: balanced lines.
A banner's air is balanced: the same room above the title as below the last row. A scroll cue sits on the controls row, at the left, never on a line of its own.
A menu column does not change on hover: no when-asked tags, no lighting and dimming. The hover is the row under the pointer, nothing else.
A hover rule (the red line that draws on hover) runs along the FOOT of a card or tile, everywhere on the site.
A picture tile rests a little grey and comes to full colour under the pointer. No zoom on hover.
Tiles in a set are equal. No outsized first tile.
An arrow stands alone: no circle behind it, no box behind an icon, no square within a square.
Nothing that cannot be clicked reacts to the pointer: no lift, no light, no rule on a card that is not a link. A card that animates on its own needs no hover.
No icon in a circle, no dashed ring, no dot-dot-dot decoration. Where an icon is thin, use the more detailed drawing.

The Services facility map: the front face must read clean. Done 23 Oct: the cladding joints fade with distance and go out on a pick; the picked state keeps its depth and tints only what is hidden; the building's skin never ghosts.
No eyebrow above a title unless it carries a fact. Start a conversation, Where we build and their kind are off.
A call-to-action band stacks: the title and the line on top, the button anchored bottom right, the phone at the left of the same row. The same on every page.
Every page is swept against these rules, not only the ones walked. Each change is recorded here so a design can be vetoed.

The 3D and animation get the same polish: timing, labels, the view at rest. Done 23 Oct on the district cooling tour (labels after the camera, the tank on the step's clock, stations named once, a dwell per step with a time bar, the tour ends on the overview) and on the Services map (rule 37).
Never a design that has no function: no ring, circle, line or dot put in to fill space. Density over white space: the client does not like white space; negative space only where it does a job.
On a phone a banner's headline, line and button stay together; no dead gap pushing the line to the foot.
